enonce_markdown: A mechanic uses a lever to raise one end of a car. An effort of $90\ \mathrm{N}$ overcomes a load of $450\ \mathrm{N}$. What is the mechanical advantage of the lever?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Mechanical advantage (MA) $= \dfrac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}}$. It is a ratio of two forces, so it has no unit.

### Solution

$\text{MA} = \dfrac{450\ \mathrm{N}}{90\ \mathrm{N}} = 5$.

Wrong options: $0.2$ inverts the ratio (effort divided by load); $360$ subtracts the forces; $540$ adds them. **Answer: b.**

enonce_markdown: A block and tackle pulley system has a velocity ratio of $5$. When the load rises by $0.40\ \mathrm{m}$, through what distance does the effort move?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Velocity ratio (VR) $= \dfrac{\text{distance moved by the effort}}{\text{distance moved by the load}}$.

### Solution

Distance moved by the effort $= \text{VR} \times \text{distance moved by the load} = 5 \times 0.40\ \mathrm{m} = 2.0\ \mathrm{m}$.

Wrong options: $0.08\ \mathrm{m}$ divides by VR instead of multiplying; $0.4\ \mathrm{m}$ assumes the effort moves as far as the load; $5.4\ \mathrm{m}$ adds the numbers. **Answer: c.**

enonce_markdown: A machine is used to raise a load of $800\ \mathrm{N}$ through a height of $1.5\ \mathrm{m}$. The effort is $250\ \mathrm{N}$ and it moves through a distance of $6.0\ \mathrm{m}$. What is the efficiency of the machine?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Efficiency $= \dfrac{\text{useful work output}}{\text{work input}} \times 100\,\%$, with work = force $\times$ distance moved in the direction of the force.

### Solution

Work output (on the load) $= 800\ \mathrm{N} \times 1.5\ \mathrm{m} = 1200\ \mathrm{J}$.

Work input (by the effort) $= 250\ \mathrm{N} \times 6.0\ \mathrm{m} = 1500\ \mathrm{J}$.

Efficiency $= \dfrac{1200}{1500} \times 100\,\% = 80\,\%$.

Check with the ratios: $\text{MA} = \dfrac{800}{250} = 3.2$, $\text{VR} = \dfrac{6.0}{1.5} = 4$, so $\dfrac{\text{MA}}{\text{VR}} = 0.80$.

Wrong options: $25\,\%$ uses $\dfrac{1}{\text{VR}}$ only; $32\,\%$ uses the mechanical advantage alone; $53\,\%$ forgets the distance of the load. **Answer: d.**

enonce_markdown:
A crowbar is used to lift a heavy stone. The pivot is $0.20\ \mathrm{m}$ from the load, which is $800\ \mathrm{N}$, and the effort is applied on the other side of the pivot at $1.0\ \mathrm{m}$ from it.

(a) Use the principle of moments to calculate the effort needed if the crowbar were perfect.

(b) State the velocity ratio of the crowbar.

(c) In practice the efficiency of the crowbar is $80\,\%$. Calculate the effort actually needed.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A lever balances (is in equilibrium) when clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment, with moment = force $\times$ perpendicular distance from the pivot. For any machine, $\text{efficiency} = \dfrac{\text{MA}}{\text{VR}}$, and $\text{MA} = \dfrac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}}$.

### Solution

(a) Moments about the pivot: effort $\times\ 1.0 = 800 \times 0.20$, so

$E = \dfrac{800 \times 0.20}{1.0} = 160\ \mathrm{N}$.

(b) $\text{VR} = \dfrac{\text{effort arm}}{\text{load arm}} = \dfrac{1.0}{0.20} = 5$.

(c) Efficiency $= \dfrac{\text{MA}}{\text{VR}}$, so $\text{MA} = 0.80 \times 5 = 4$.

$\text{MA} = \dfrac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}}$, so effort $= \dfrac{800}{4} = 200\ \mathrm{N}$ (more than the $160\ \mathrm{N}$ of a perfect lever, because of friction at the pivot).

enonce_markdown: A motor on a building site in Yaounde raises a load of bricks of mass $120\ \mathrm{kg}$ at constant speed through a height of $15\ \mathrm{m}$ in $20\ \mathrm{s}$. The efficiency of the hoist is $75\,\%$. Taking $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, what electrical power must be supplied to the motor?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Useful work $= mgh$; useful power $= \dfrac{\text{work}}{\text{time}}$; efficiency $= \dfrac{\text{useful power output}}{\text{power input}}$, so power input $= \dfrac{\text{useful power}}{\text{efficiency}}$.

### Solution

Useful work done on the bricks $= mgh = 120 \times 10 \times 15 = 18\,000\ \mathrm{J}$.

Useful power $= \dfrac{18\,000\ \mathrm{J}}{20\ \mathrm{s}} = 900\ \mathrm{W}$.

Power supplied $= \dfrac{900\ \mathrm{W}}{0.75} = 1200\ \mathrm{W}$.

Wrong options: $120\ \mathrm{W}$ uses mass instead of weight ($mh$ without $g$); $675\ \mathrm{W}$ multiplies by the efficiency instead of dividing; $900\ \mathrm{W}$ ignores the efficiency. **Answer: d.**

enonce_markdown:
A loader pushes a drum of weight $1500\ \mathrm{N}$ up a straight ramp $4.0\ \mathrm{m}$ long onto the back of a lorry whose floor is $1.0\ \mathrm{m}$ above the ground. He pushes with a constant force of $500\ \mathrm{N}$ parallel to the ramp.

(a) Calculate the useful work done in raising the drum, and the work done by the loader.

(b) Calculate the efficiency of the ramp.

(c) Calculate the mechanical advantage and the velocity ratio of the ramp.

(d) Assuming all the wasted energy is used against friction between the drum and the ramp, calculate the frictional force.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Work = force $\times$ distance moved in the direction of the force. Efficiency $= \dfrac{\text{work output}}{\text{work input}}$. For an inclined plane, $\text{VR} = \dfrac{\text{length of slope}}{\text{vertical height}}$ and $\text{MA} = \dfrac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}}$. Wasted energy $=$ work input $-$ useful work output.

### Solution

(a) Useful work $= 1500\ \mathrm{N} \times 1.0\ \mathrm{m} = 1500\ \mathrm{J}$ (the drum is raised vertically by $1.0\ \mathrm{m}$).

Work done by the loader $= 500\ \mathrm{N} \times 4.0\ \mathrm{m} = 2000\ \mathrm{J}$ (he pushes along the whole length of the ramp).

(b) Efficiency $= \dfrac{1500}{2000} \times 100\,\% = 75\,\%$.

(c) $\text{MA} = \dfrac{1500}{500} = 3$ and $\text{VR} = \dfrac{4.0}{1.0} = 4$. Check: $\dfrac{\text{MA}}{\text{VR}} = \dfrac{3}{4} = 75\,\%$.

(d) Energy wasted $= 2000 - 1500 = 500\ \mathrm{J}$. This is the work done against friction over the $4.0\ \mathrm{m}$ of the ramp:

$f \times 4.0 = 500 \Rightarrow f = \dfrac{500}{4.0} = 125\ \mathrm{N}$.
